On the Orders of the Day:

May I ask my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, what is the object of the present conference in Ottawa between the delegates of the West Indies and the Canadian Government? Is the object purely a commercial one, or is there something else?

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
The object is briefly as follows: In 1912, a conference was held which resulted in the arrangement of a ten years' reciprocal trade agreement between Canada and the West Indies. That agreement has still two years to run. Transport and cable facilities were also arranged for at the same conference. It has been considered wise that we should meet together a little in advance of the time when the old arrangement would expire, to take into consideration exactly the same subjects, so what is being considered, and what will be considered, at the present conference is, first, the trade relations of the two sections of the Empire as regards preference and objects or lists of preference; second, the improvement of transport facilities, both as to passengers and freights, making them

more uniform, and, if possible, more widely distributed, and more commodious; third, the improvement of cable facilities, which have been very poor during the past year or two, and which it is necessary to have improved in the interests of trade and communication. Those are the three matters, and those alone, which are under consideration.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speechtext:
The House resumed, from Friday, May 28, the debate , on the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for t/he House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. W. S. Fielding.
Hon. T. A. CREE.AR (Marquette): Mr. Speaker, in rising to make my contribution to the debate on the Budget, let me say at the outset that I hope to detain the House for no very great length of time. We have been debating the matter now for almost two weeks and naturally there remains little that can be added to the discussion that has already taken place. Before I come to discuss the proposals outlined in the speech delivered by the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), I wish to refer briefly to some of the criticisms directed against our Progressive group at this end of the Chamber by some hon. members on the other side of the House.
I have in mind particularly at the present time the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who spoke for almost two hours in this Chamber and, during the greater part of his speech, endeavoured to describe, or to criticise, certain actions of the grain growers and the farmers, which certainly was not relevant to the subject of debate. The criticisms were, I might add, very fg,r wide of the mark indeed.
My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) seems to be very much exercised over the continuation of the Canada Wheat Board. He attributes the formation of that board, and the effort to maintain it, to the farmers of

this country. I believe he even suggested that some of the members who sit behind me were desirous of seeing this board continued. Well in that regard, I am expressing my own personal opinion, and I think the opinion of those who sit around me, when I say that Government control in matters of this kind is not desirable as a permanent policy. My hon. friend, however, saw fit to take a different position. He apparently is quite desirous that this control shall cease at the earliest possible moment. I would suggest to him that he consult the Government as to what their policy for the future in the matter is. It does not lie with members on this side of the House, nor does it lie with the members particularly sitting around me, to say what the policy of the Government is to be in this respect. I would suggest to my hon. friend that if he is very anxious that this control should cease he might consult the chairman of the Committee on Agriculture of the House of Commons who, I understand, is strongly in favour of the continuation of the board. I would also suggest that he keep his eye on the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) and the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) because if he does he may learn that the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Immigration and Colonization are perhaps now harbouring the thought of maintaining this control as a peimanent policy in order that they can appeal to the farmers of Canada with it as an offset to their tariff demands. I would suggest that consideration to my hon. friend.
My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) also saw fit to refer to the profits that had been made by the farmers' organizations and particularly that one with which I am associated. I do not know that this is a subject that is of much interest in this debate to the members of the House. I desire to say, however, that I will be very glad indeed to give my hon. friend, at any time, all the information he desires on that point and I certainly hope it will lead him to a more correct understanding than that which he displayed in his criticism. His criticism, based upon the statement that a profit of 211 per cent was made by the terminal elevator operated by the United Grain Growers, is altogether wide of the mark. This elevator is leased from the Canadian Pacific railway and -I wish to point out to my hon. friend if he wishes to be fair in the matter that back of that there is an investment of over $2,000,000 in country elevators for the purpose of gathering the grain that is sent to this terminal elevator. lIf my hon. friend wishes to be fair he must take that into account in any criticism he makes of it.
He also referred to the profits made by the Grain Growers Export Company of New York, a subject which also furnished a fruitful topic to the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards). It is true we have an export company in New York. It is organized under the New York state laws. It is true that with a capital of $100,000 the company earned $500,000 in 1915. But the explanation lies in this, that the company enjoyed exceptional privileges of credit. Our bank loans ran very high and the total amount of grain that was handled and which furnished the profit mentioned, was over 86,000,000 bushels. I ask my hon. friend if less than one-half of one per cent on the turn-over which was the fact in this case is an excessive profit. If my hon. friend wants to be fair I would suggest this other consideration, Mr. Speaker: I do not like at any time to parade before the public my patriotism or the patriotism of my friends but I think it may be interesting to my hon. friend to know that when the stress and trouble in connection with food supplies came upon us, when the Allies centralized their organization in Europe and extended their organization in America to handle grain, the Grain Growers Export Company, these profiteers whom my hon. friend described, turned over for absolutely nothing in return, their whole organization to the Wheat Export Company representing the British Government in New York, and for twenty-two months we served that organization with no return save salaries and expenses. We purchased and forwarded on ocean vessels for them over 197,000,000 bushels of oats and as I have said, we got not one cent out of it.
My hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) also had something to say the other night, He, at any rate, spoke with a certainty of knowledge that leaves no doubt of conviction in his own mind regardless of whether he is able to successfully convince other members in the House.

Another very important
announcement in the Budget was the Government's policy on the tariff question. For a long time there had been considerable doubt in the public mind as to where the Government were eventually going to land in the matter of a tariff policy; and there was a good deal of heart searching and anxiety on the part of a good many of my hon. friends apposite-the member for Simoce North (Mr. Currie) for instance, and several others. But whatever struggle may have gone on behind the scenes, the matter is now settled; at any rate, we must accept the declaration of policy made by the Minister of Finance. Undoubtedly there were two conflicting elements among the Government's supporters in regard to this question:	There were those who believe
in a low tariff policy; there were those who believe in a policy of adequate protection.
And I can well conceive the difficulties of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) and my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) in reaching a decision upon the question, for during the period



that has elapsed since last autumn, when a declaration of policy was looked for, considerable water has run under the bridge. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) has made some speeches throughout the country in an endeavour to feel out the public on this matter. Down in Quebec he told the shoe manufacturers: "We must have a policy of adequate protection for Canadian industries." In Kingston a little later he was speaking in favour of "moderate" protection.

He says that the balance has been made up in this way:
First: Shipping freights. Our ships carry goods to and from them all over the world.
If Britain had been following a protectionist policy for the last seventy years, would her ships be going into every harbour and port of the world? Without any question they would not.
Second: Interest coupons. The American securities held by English investors yield a constant income in interest, to meet which the United States has to send goods.
My hon. friend practically stated that the other night, but he made this other remarkable statement: that it was the accumulated wealth of Great Britain prior to 1850 that had enabled her to make these investments in foreign countries and thus to overcome the handicaps that free trade had brought to her. There is one other item that helps to make up the balance:
Third: Insurance facilities. The English insurance companies and firms do a large business in the United States and draw thence a regular income in premiums.
Another result of the free trade policy of Great Britain. Then, banking facilities. Why, it is a well known fact that London was the international clearing house for the business of the world; that there was not a bank or a broker in London who did not take toll in some form

of the business of the world. The United States a protected country! If the United States wanted to pay for goods bought in China, she invariably did so by a draft on London; and it was the toll thus taken, the commissions and premiums earned on these transactions, that adjusted the balance o'f trade. I cannot for the life of me understand why my hon. friend bases his argument on the adverse balance of trade of Great Britain. We have a good example in Switzerland.	I am told that
Switzerland has nearly always had an adverse balance of trade, yet it is one of the most prosperous countries in Europe. Therefore, the argument that an adverse balance of trade is necesarily bad for a country does not hold water.

Now, the hon. gentleman also speaks about the decline in the value of farm lands in the United Kingdom, and he compares that country with the United States and Canada during the last seventy years. Of course, there has been a tremendous increase in the total value of farm lands in the United States and Canada during the last fifty years. Why? The country was opening up and new lands were being brought under cultivation, with the result that the aggregate increase in wealth in this respect was very marked. But that is scarcely a fair basis of comparison to take for the United Kingdom. Canada and the United States are new countries and they are not finished countries. Although agriculture may not be very prosperous in Canada we have added to the sum total of the value of cultivated agricultural land because we have new people coming and opening up new land all the time.
My hon. friend also quoted the values of farm lands in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia. I do not know from what source his figures were secured but they did strike me as being rather high. He tells us that in British Columbia farm lands have advanced from $74 in 1910 to $174 per acre in 1919, and if I remember his statement aright, in Nova Scotia there has been a considerable increase in farm land values also. I am free to say to my hon. friend that there has been an increase in value in the farm lands of the Prairie Provinces and possibly of British Columbia and the Maritime Provinces as well, but one of the factors in producing that increase is that we have had opened up to us the United States market for Canadian farm products. The argument was advanced, and I think it was advanced with reason, that the reciprocity arrangement suggested in 1911 would add $5 an acre to the value of our farm lands in Western Canada that were producing grain. Well this is one of the reasons for the increase. If my hon. friend goes to the Maritime Provinces he will find that they have a free market in the United States for their potatoes, for their apples, for all classes of agricultural products, whereas, a few years ago, they had to climb over a high tariff wall to get into that country. The result has been to increase the prosperity of the farmers in the Maritime Provinces.

speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman in favour of making apples free?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Certainly, I am in favour of making apples free. My hon. friend from Annapolis is badly mistaken if he thinks he is putting a poser to me in that regard. My hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) also quoted very largely from the reports of the special committees that were appointed by the Asquith Government to investigate trade conditions in the United Kingdom. It is true these committees were appointed in 1916 and that they were appointed by a Government of which Mr. Asquith was the head. But it was a coalition government; it was not the old Liberal Government in Great Britain. A coalition had been formed in 1915 and there were in that government quite a number of people who had held conflicting tariff views just as I fancy there has been in the Government of Canada in the making of the present Budget. But the fact that -these committees brought in these reports, I submit, is no substantial evidence to support the contention of my hon. friend that free trade has been a failure in Great Britain. Take the committee on iron and steel that he referred to. The report of that committee was dissented from by Sir Hugh Bell, who is one of the greatest iron masters in northern England and who is at the head of one of the biggest iron and steel firms in the United Kingdom. If Sir Hugh Bell took the position that duties on iron and steel coming into the United Kingdom were not desirable, why did he do so? He is a manufacturer; only he could benefit. When that question was put to my hon. friend he said in effect, in reply, that Sir Hugh Bell was wedded to tradition, that he could not get over his old free trade ideas and that in order to stick to them he would rather sacrifice his own financial benefit. I have done business with business men in the United Kingdom and I have never met a harder headed lot of business men any where than I have found in Great Britain. When my hon. friend suggests that the greatest iron master and manufacturer in Great Britain refused to do a thing that would be beneficial to his business simply because he was wedded to tradition his argument rests upon a ridiculous basis. The fact is that Sir Hugh Bell knows that in the long run, duties on iron and steel coming into the United Kingdom would not be in the interest of the iron industry.
I am free to say there is one respect in which the United Kingdom has perhaps lagged behind. It has lagged behind in the matter of technical education. The superiority that Germany and the United States acquired in some fields of manufacture was

due not to their fiscal policy but due very largely to the fact that they had provided in these countries the very finest technical schools that could be found anywhere. They applied chemistry and science to their manufactures in a way that the British manufacturer and business man did not do. But now the tale is changed; Great Britain, as a result of the war, certainly realizes the advantage of technical education and I venture to say will soon bring it within the reach of her people.
I submit again that these committees were appointed at a time of war fervour. The resolutions passed at the Paris conference, I think, in 1916, laid it down as a principle that the Allies would not renew trade with Germany when the war was over. But they have seen the futility of that position and it is not a fair or sound argument to take the reports of these committees that were appointed at that time as evidence of a need of protection in Great Britain. But what has happened to these reports? Where have they gone? These committees were appointed in 1916 and they brought in their reports in 1918. Since that time Mr. Austen Chamberlain, the son of the only British statesman who ever endeavoured to fasten protection in a limited form on the British people in the last seventy years, has brought in two Budgets. Has he made any reference to the reports of these committees? Has he suggested a duty on iron, steel or textiles? He certainly has not. I think we are well aware that in 1918 shortly after the last British election, an effort was made to introduce into the fiscal system of Great Britain anti-dumping duties. What response did it find? There was not a reputable statesman in Great Britain who would take it up and the result was that nothing has been heard of it and I venture to say nothing will be heard of it. I want to read to the House the concluding statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) in his disquisition on the fallacies of free trade as found in Great Britain. This, to my mind, is an amazing statement; I cannot characterize it in any other words. What does he say?
We are at a stage now where we cannot mistake the teachings of experience. We have seen the result through seventy years in the Old Land. It is traced in the history of their trade returns that turned in 1850, the last decade year when they had a balance in their favour, and every decade year since a balance against them. Free trade has depopulated rural England ; it has filled the emigrant ships with fugitives from her shores; It has scattered the manhood of Great Britain through the fields and workshops of the United States; it has starved and repressed and dwarfed the nascent indus-
[Mr. Cre:'a.r. j
tries of Ireland ; it has reversed the supremacy that Britain held through centuries in the industrial life of the world, and caused her to concede the place to other great competing nations that adopted a different policy. Such is the history of free trade.
To my mind-and I say it in the best of good temper-the Minister of the Interior has never made a more amazing statement than the one I have just quoted. Why, Mr. Speaker, we have just come out of a war that has stressed and tried every country in the world, and what is the result? Where is protectionist Germany to-day? Where is protectionist France and where is protectionist Italy? Where are they- where are they financially? Where does their currency stand in the exchanges of the world? To say that Great Biitain is decadent, in the face of the fact that she not only financed her own part in the war, which was teriffic, but loaned to her Allies over $8,000,000,000 during the war-why, Sir, the thing is beyond belief. If the war has proven anything it has proven the efficacy of the fiscal policy of Great Britain and her financial stability. My hon. friend talks about the depopulation of Great Britain, and the people fleeing from her shores to new pastures! Why, the population of Great Britain increased between 1850 and 1911 from twenty-seven millions to forty-five millions,

First I will take Gladstone. Was Gladstone a protectionist? Did he believe in protection? Did Campbell-Bannerman, Asquith and Lloyd George believe in protection? My hon. friends opposite may say, "These were Liberals and nothing else was to be expected of them." Well, we will take Conservative statesmen in Great Britain, and with the exception of Joseph Chamberlain, and even-he made it clear, in his tariff reform propaganda in Great Britain about seventeen or eighteen years ago, that he had no use for protection as protection; his campaign and arguments were based altogether on creating Imperial preferences in order to hold the Empire together. I think he was mistaken in that, but nevertheless he is on record as saying that he did not believe in protection for protection's sake. What about Peel, the Duke of Devonshire, and Lord St. Aldwyn. The last named, as Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, was one of the great English chancellors. What about Lord Salisbury and Lord Robert Cecil and Lord Hugh Cecil? Were these men carried away by the glamour of protection? No, they were absolutely against it. What about the Right Honourable A. J. Balfour, perhaps the
brightest intellect in the Conservative party in Great Britain? He refused to follow Chamberlain in his protectionist propaganda and policy. What about Disraeli, the creator of the modern Tory party in Great Britain? His judgment on protection was that so far as Great Britain was concerned it was not only dead but damned.

speechtext: That is being done to-day under this very Budget.

speechtext: In Great Britain, the Minister of the Interior tells us, they are raising a billion and a half dollars this year from customs taxation. I think he is mistaken in the figures, but at any rate they are raising a very large amount in customs taxes. We can still get a great deal of revenue from the tariff in Canada, and at the same time eliminate the principle of protection in industry, which is bad. That is the thing we should do. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have continued at much greater length than I intended, but I have yet a few further observations to make.

speechtext: Give them more of it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I submit -that the whole argument, as far as the fiscal policy of Great Britain is concerned, confirms absolutely, unequivocally, and beyond successful contradiction, that that policy has been in the interests of the United Kingdom, and I submit that a similar policy in Canada could do nothing but redound to the benefit of this Dominion. What have been the effects of protection in Canada? We have a perfect right to ask what benefit has it been to the country? Is it a sensible thing to develop artificial industries and make it difficult for the natural industries of the country to develop? We say we want to develop agriculture. Would my hon. friends opposite say that we should protect agriculture by way of giving a bounty to the wheat producers of Western Canada?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Yes, if it needs it.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I do not know where, in the end, my hon. friend would get the money. Agriculture is the basic industry of this country, and it is the part of wisdom to free the tools of production that are necessary for the development of this great industry, and the development of our forests, our mines, and our fisheries as well. I have never been able to see the sense of creating, for instance, a cotton industry in Canada-which I shall refer to in a moment-and which is entirely an artificial industry in this country We do not produce the raw material that enters into the manufacture of textiles in this country, but we have to import every ounce of that raw material. Is it not in every sense a better thing to produce the articles that we can best produce in this country, and that are natural to the country, and trade them off to others for things they can produce better than we can? That is the sensible policy to follow.
Now, what is the position of agriculture in this country? The farmers of Western Canada are producing two staple commodities, grain and livestock, and the basis of value upon which they sell their productions is fixed in the markets of the world. You will have to have protection in Canada for a long time before you can have a market capable of consuming all the wheat our farmers produce. But they are not afraid to sell their wheat against all comers; and the same holds good in regard to livestock.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I do not wish to be interrupted. You are putting a

penalty on agriculture when you say to the farmers: "You must have the cost of your implements of production increased by the operation of this Customs tariff." You are making it more difficult for agriculture to succeed, and to that extent you are hampering and handicapping an industry that is natural to the country. We talk of Canada being an agricultural country. Of course it is. And eventually it will become a great manufacturing country; there is not any question about that. But if we develop agriculture, if we can put 2,000,000 farmers on the land, will not that be a good thing for our manufacturers? I can conceive of nothing better for creating a home market.
But the fact is that to-day agriculture is carried on under conditions of disadvantage. I will admit that during the last few years where farmers have secured good crops they have made money. But go out and speak to the farmers of Southern Alberta, who have had three successive crop failures; go out and speak to the farmers of Southern Saskatchewan, who have had the same misfortune; go out and speak to the farmers of Eastern Canada who have been handicapped by bad crops, and ask them what their opinion is of having the cost of the tools and implements of their industry added to by the operation of the Customs tariff; it will not take you long to get a reply.
During this debate we have heard some comment on our textile industry, and my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) placed upon Hansard some figures in connection with the development of that industry in this country. But he did not supply all the information on the subject at that time. The Dominion Textile Company, Limited, is our leading concern manufacturing cotton goods, and is a combination of four textile companies that were merged in 1905. At that time-and this is taken from the evidence given by the General Manager of the Dominion Textile Company, Limited before the Cost of Living Commission a year ago-his company issued $5,000,000 of common stock for which they paid $500,000, or $10 a share, thus four and a half millions of that common stock was pure water. What happened? Under the shelter of the tariff, enjoying protective duties ranging from 30 to 40 per cent, the Dominion Textile Company, Limited, was able to so extract profits from the people of this country that this stock last year was quoted as high as $125 a share. I ask my hon. friend the Minister

of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), who, I believe, stated at Quebec that the tariff should not be used as a place of shelter by industries that could stand on their own feet, what he thinks of that condition of affairs?

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman want an answer? I understand that in that case the profits were made largely out of export trade as a result of the war.

speechtext: Well, we can go back to 1914, before the war, and we shall find that this $5,000,000 of common stock, or rather $4,500,000, that in 1905 had no value whatever, in 1914 was selling as high as $86 a share. If my hon. friend will study the figures of our exports at that time he will find that very litle business was done in Canadian textiles. And yet that $4,500,000 of common stock, of pure unadulterated water, had attained a value of over $3,000,000! Is that building up useful industry in this country, or is it not enriching the few at the expense of the many? But by way of contrast, what are the wages paid to our textile workers in Canada? According to figures from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics 7,946 males and 7,654 females, or a total of 15,618, are engaged in the cotton textile industry in this country. Now I wish' to direct the attention of the House to this illuminating fact, that the average yearly wage of those 15,000 employees is only $538.23. Is that what protection has done for the workers of our textile industry?

speechtext:
There must be a basis
for that average.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
It is based on returns supplied by companies covering all the textile industries in this country. Will any one argue that that is a reasonable condition of affairs? If my hon. friends want a moderate tariff for revenue only, and if the Government desire to wipe out special privilege in this direction, why did they not start on the tariff schedule in respect to cotton goods when arranging their Budget? On the contrary, these cotton duties are maintained. And the same condition applies not only to the textile industry, but to many other industries as well.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the tariff views of this little group are well known. As I have stated before, we stand broadly on this principle,-that the implements of production for the development of our agriculture, our forests, our mines, and our fisheries should be made free, and that there should be a substantial reduction in all other duties under the general tariff. That is a specific plank in the platform of the Council of Agriculture. I want to know what are the views of my hon. friend opposite on this question. I would like the Minister of the Interior in his next speech, or the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, to state his views as to what duties should prevail on, say, agricultural implements, on textiles, and on iron and coal.
We have read a good deal in the papers recently about the British Empire Steel merger. Mr. Grant Morden who is a member of the British House of Commons but Canadian born, I am told at a meeting in this city recently made the statement,-that this merger, when completed, would be in a position to compete with the world. Well, if that be the case, would it not be a good thing to remove the duty on coal and so help the manufacturers and other consumers in the province of Ontario who are using coal, and would it not be a good thing to take the duty off iron and steel as well? I cannot for the life of me, Sir, see the advantage of supporting a policy that develops mergers, such as the British Empire Steel merger, which is practically cornering all the coal and iron ore in sight in the Maritime Provinces and with the inevitable result of an effort being made with the assistance of the tariff to pay dividends on large amounts of watered stock.
I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that one of the most effective ways in which he can combat this growing tendency to combine various companies into huge combinations is by using the weapon of the tariff. The tariff has been used not only in the industries I have mentioned, but it has been used in many others that could be mentioned by company promoters simply for the purpose of taking additional profits out of the Canadian people. I make the statement in all seriousness that the protective tariff has been the greatest agency for exploiting our people that was ever devised.
I want to give the Minister of Finance further evidence. For instance, moulded rubber goods are used largely in this country. I gave this statement to the House on a previous occasion but I repeat it again because it is pertinent to the matter we are discussing. The following is taken from a prospectus issued by the K. & 8. Canadian Tire and Rubber Company, Limited, of Toronto, circulated privately for the pur-

pose of getting additional money to put into their business-and I am using this quotation because it is direct evidence, not hearsay; it is from a prospectus issued by these people themselves:
At Weston, Ontario, we have the only plant in Canada for making moulded rubber goods exclusively. Our capacity amounts to 3,000 pieces per day. This class of goods in the past has been imported principally from the States. It would not be policy to state our margin of profit, but believe that we are able to manufacture at United States costs.
Now, note this:
There is a protective tariff of at least 35 per cent (and up to 42J per cent) in our favour. We are thus able to sell at a lower price than any foreign competitor and still have a good profit.
The quality of our rubber sundries is admitted to be the equal of the best imported goods.
Will any of my hon. friends opposite argue for a moment that the K. & S. Canadian Tire and Rubber Company, who, on their own admission, can manufacture as cheaply in Canada as they do in the United States, are selling these goods at prices any lower than the prices of similar goods imported from the United States? I will tell you more. The Minister of Finance will probably find an effort being made one of these days to mergerize the rubber companies of this country who are manufacturing rubber goods; they will capitalize their earning power and issue a lot of common stock against it, which will represent no value, and in order to do it more effectively they will get under the shelter of the protective tariff. I would commend these considerations to the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance.
Now, I have spoken somewhat longer than I had intended. Out views on the question of tariff are well known; I have already stated them. I want to say a word about the amendment that my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has moved. I quite agree with the member from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) that the amendment has considerable milk and water. The plain fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker is, that the time has oome when we should get away from all make-believe on this question of tariff. We are entitled to know where every one stands in this matter. I have every respect for the man who honestly holds the view that protection is necessary for this country. But we want a clear cut discussion of the question, and I hope that my hon. friends opposite, when the time comes that the tariff [Mr. Crerar-l
is discussed in the open forum, will debate the question on its merits and
5 p.m. not seek to cloak and cover it up with various other appeals to racial and religious prejudices, as has so often been the case in the past. What we	want is to get a
clear, definite expression of opinion from the Canadian people upon the question. In this period of reconstruction, when we are confronted with gigantic problems, questions of tariff and of business administration certainly call for closer study than has ever been the case in the past. We can only overcome, I am convinced, the financial difficulties which confront us and lighten the financial burdens that the Canadian people have to carry, by an intelligent development of the resources of this country, and I again submit that of all these resources the one that lies most readily to hand is that of our agriculture. Let us, Mr. Speaker, direct our policy in the future to the development of these industries instead of seeking to create artificial industries that have to live under the sheltering wing of a high protective tariff. Let us seek to develop the industries that are natural to the country; if we do, the development of other industries will follow as surely as night follows day. By adopting a policy of this kind; by adopting a policy of special privileges to none-because I submit that the tariff is a special privilege to those who have the benefit of it-we shall lay firm and broad the foundations of a great and prosperous country.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before attempting to follow the arguments of the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House (Mr. Crerar), I would like to say that the Budget presented to Parliament this year reminds us that although the war is ended, war conditions are to some extent still with us. A crisis in our history has been reached and safely passed. But we have still great obligations to meet, and I am sure that the people of Canada will prove themselves capable of dealing with those obligations. I listened with a great deal of interest to the first Budget Speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and I must congratulate him upon the manner in which he delivered it, upon the conciseness with which he dealt with the various matters connected with it, and upon the frank and open manner in which he revealed to the people the exact financial situation as it is and as it has to be dealt with.	.

That Canada is a difficult country to govern I believe everybody realizes. Under ordinary conditions, in the absence ol such problems as have to be dealt with at the present time, the Government of Canada, is most difficult. But the present situation is much less serious than it was two years ago. I am particularly pleased to know that we have with us again the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) who carried on during the whole period of the war; the man who, by his wonderful foresight, endeavoured to have Canada prepared as well as was possible when the terrible war broke loose upon the world. He carried on during the early years of the war and year after year as the war continued. We were, however, put to a crucial test in the fall of 1-917, when the question arose whether the people of Canada would uphold the policy of the Prime Minister and his Government. Notwithstanding the fact that 400,000 Canadians had gone overseas; notwithstanding the fact that there was a casualty list of over 125,000, the mandate which he received and which the Government received on that occasion was to carry on. He carried on, and he saw the war brought to a successful conclusion. He has been subjected to considerable criticism, not only by hon. members opposite but from other sources outside of this House, because he was not day in and day out on the job here in Canada. We welcome him back to the forum of Parliament. We are plea-sed indeed to know, and the people of Canada rejoice in it, that Sir Robert Borden is again able to carry on, and likely to do so for many years.
We have listened for about an hour -and a half to an hon. gentleman who was a member of the Cabinet when Sir Robert Borden and his Government received that mandate in the fall of 1917. A year -ago we heard him -address this House and endeavour to explain to the people why he had broken with the Government. There has been a good deal of speculation in regard to that matter, not only by hon. members here, but by the people throughout the country. Now he -appears in the role of leader of a party in this House, and if under those conditions I h-ave something to -say -that he may consider as rather unkind it is because of the fact that the situation is a very peculiar one and not from any -personal motive, it is absolutely necessary and in the public interest that we should have a united people to deal with the task which lies before us as one whole people with a common ideal, and not
in sections, not divided into classes and factions. We must unite the whole people of this country, and when- we do that, we shall overcome the difficulties we have to contend with so quickly that in a few years from now I venture to state that the people will wonder how it was that there was any alarm felt in this Parliament or outside of it over the debt now confronting us.
I was somewhat startled to hear the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Trahan) in his speech in this House on the 28th instant, referring to the debt which we have on our shoulders, protest against the policy embodied in the slogan which was adopted in the last election that we were in the war "To the last man and the last dollar," till our efforts were crowned with victory. He went on to state that the policy adopted by the Government was to place British interests first and Canadian interests in a secondary position. Now I want to take strong exception to that statement. We are a part of the British Empire. We have not yet reached that stage, nor do we intend to reach it, when our connection with the Empire will be severed. It was well known that at that time the fate of the Empire was almost hanging in the balance, and it was realized we were a part, of the Empire. The hon. member then went on to compare our debt with that of Japan, and he quoted figures to show that our obligations were much heavier than those of Japan. He even suggested that Ja-pan had acquitted herself and rendered a service during the war equally as great as did Canada. I take exception to any statement of that kind. I am not one of those who believe in continually referring to what -Canada did in the war. Canada's part in the war is a matter o:f history, and- is well known. I believe that the consensus of opinion throughout the world is that Canada acquitted herself in a manner to which no one could take any exception, and the obligations which we have to face as a result of our effort in the war .are no greater than could be expected.
I wish to refer briefly to some of the statements made by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). For about an hour he spoke on the tariff. He laboured long along that line, and practically advocated free trade until almost the concluding sentences of his address, when, questioned from this side of the House as to where he stood, he hesitated, and then referred .to the platform of the United Grain Growers-	.

of the Council of Agriculture. I was also surprised to see, immediately after the Minister of Finance had concluded his Budget speech, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) spring to his feet ae iif he were afraid some one else would catch the Speaker's eye. In concluding the address he delivered, following that of the Minister of Finance, he moved an amendment which was evidently prepared before he had heard or knew anything about what the Budget speech contained. That was quite evident to every one who heard him, and it is little wonder that he has been taunted by some hon. gentlemen opposite as to the small quantity of milk his amendment really contains compared with the water. But the most remarkable feature of his address was that he advocated protection, advocated the dumping clause, and also favoured mergers. He cautioned the people of this country to take little stock in the platform of either the Liberal party or that of hon. gentlemen on the cross benches. He cautioned the people of this country not to be led away with any idea that the Liberal party were likely to put into effect the platform they had adopted. He said that the responsibility of office had a sobering effect, and consequently the people need not be frightened by what the Grain Growers are likely to do should they come into power, and as he spoke I could not help feeling that while there may not be any very good team work on this side of the House there is considerable between the two Oppositions we have represented in this House. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, -whose speech has been so severely criticized, judging from his past history, might well caution the people of Canada not to take those platforms too seriously but I say that this is a time when we should take politics, seriously in this country, I am very much mistaken indeed, and I am inclined to think that some of these hon. gentlemen, old and experienced in political life as they may be, will find they have made a great mistake if they think the people can be fooled along that line much longer. I do not want to do the hon. gentleman an injustice. This is what he said:
I do not think myself, as things are going now, that we can look to that party-
That is the party led by the hon. member for Marquette.
-for a sound tariff policy. What then? I do not even think we can expect to get a sound and safe tariff policy hy a too rigid adherence
[Mr. Gould.)
to every line and every letter of the Liberal tariff platform. I think myself that we will find that we are all prone in framing platforms to put things perhaps a little more strongly than is wise and we all find when we come to the responsibilities of office that we may have to modify our views. If we are to get a sound and sane tariff policy where shall we look for it?
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) in his address in this House the other day quoted from a speech made by the leader of the Liberal party previous to the elections of 1896. He quoted Sir Wilfrid Laurier as saying:
I submit to you that the ideal fiscal system is the British system of free trade.
I come to expose to you the policy of the Liberal party. Let me tell you that the policy may be summed up in the good Saxon word " Freedom," in every sense of the term-freedom of speech, freedom of action, freedom of religious life and civil life, and last, not least, freedom in commercial life. I denounce to you the policy of protection as bondage.
Those were the statements made by the leader of the Opposition of that day, in giving his policy with regard to the tariff. A short time afterwards he got into power, he later on delivered a speech in the manufacturing industrial city of Toronto in 1906, in which he is reported by the Toronto Globe to have said:
Everybody will agree with me, the business men of Toronto more than anybody-that in a fiscal policy such as we have, where we derive our revenue chiefly from customs duties, it is absolutely essential to the capitalist, to the workingman, to the businessman, to the industrialist, that he should know exactly the conditions under which he invests his capital; that he should know that it will be invested under a condition that will not be lightly altered.
These would appear to be the words of a man who was conscious of the responsibility of office whidh had been placed upon his shoulders. He then went on in his speech to deal with what- he characterized as the tinkering with the tariff which had been done by the Conservative Government previous to 1896, when the Liberal party came into power.	I could
give the number of changes he referred to in that address, but I will not delay the House to do so. After having done that, he said:
Well, sir, when there were so many changes the manufacturer dreaded the day of the Budget Speech. He was always anxious lest he find himself the following morning a ruined man. But I am proud to say that under our regime the manufacturers always sleep soundly and never fear interference with the tariff. We have made very few changes in the duty.
It goes on to bear out the statement that was made by the hon. member for Mar-

quette (Mr. Crerar) that we have and have had in this country, under both the Conservative party and the Liberal party, the old National Policy. There is no getting away from that. The National Policy was amended time and again before Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power, but he ad-milts in that speech delivered in Toronto that very few changes had been made in the tariff by his party. Changes are continually necessary, Mr. Speaker, because conditions change in a country as time goes on; and a tariff that might be suitable to the requirements of the country at this stage might not be suitable a few years hence. But I think that every one will agree that under the extraordinary war conditions such as we have experienced, what we required was stability and confidence on the part of every individual; and it will be conceded, I think, that we required also that the greatest possible effort should be put forth by all the people, and it was not by any such means as have been alluded to this afternoon by the hon. membeT for Marquette that the condition which we desired could be brought about.
Now, Sir, I am coming to the time when the hon. member for Marquette, who I regret is not in his seat, saw fit to break with the Government, and I shall deal briefly with the reasons which he gave for parting company with them on that occasion. I have here a copy of the letter which he sent to the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) in reference to the matter, in which he states:
Ottawa, June 4th, 1919.
You will observe, before I proceed any further, Mr. Speaker, that the Budget Speech was delivered the following day. The hon. member remained in the Government until the moment when the Budget was to be introduced. Apparently, the matter had been settled. The hon. member wrote as follows:
My dear Sir Robert,-The Government in its consideration of the Budget to be placed before Parliamerit to-morrow has reached, I take it, definite and final conclusions as to the form it will take. As you are aware, I am not in accord with it and therefore cannot support it either in the House or in the country. Having reached this decision, there is only one course for me to follow, and I therefore tender you herewith my resignation as a member of the Government. The reason for my decision shall be given more fully when the subject is under discussion in the House.
It was the question of the tariff upon which the hon. member for Marquette broke with the Government. Let me remind the
House that the tariff was not an issue in the election of 1917. So far as I am aware, there was no discussion in connection with tariff issues in any part of the country at that time. It was recognized that men of different views concerning the tariff had joined together and that we had established a union or coalition government to carry on during the war and throughout the reconstruction period afterwards. It is true that changes were made in the tariff in 1919. When the Budget was brought down it was found that in regard to the very things that have been advocated by the hon. member (Mr. Crerar) to-day as items that should be placed on the free list, a fairly generous concession had been made in that direction. The tariff had been reduced on a great many agricultural implements from 17j per cent to 12J per cent, and the surtax of 1915 of 7\ per cent, had also been removed. Better rates for shipment of machinery over the railways of the country so far as Western Canada was concerned had also been obtained, and the Government had done the very thing which hon. gentleman had been advocating. Notwithstanding that there had been no reference to the tariff in the election of 1917, the Government conceded to hon. members from Western Canada something along the line which they have advocated. The Government met them more than half way, but the hon. member (Mr. Crerar) found even then that he had to devise some excuse to leave the Government. I do not think his explanation has satisfied the members of this House, nor do I think it has satisfied the people of the country. The hon. member is leader of a political party in this country to-day, and consequently we are justified in examining his actions and his words and also in endeavouring to arrive at some understanding as to what his motives are and the influence which controls him. The statement has been made by a member of the Government-and it has nolt been denied by any one-that the Government were agreed to go on as they were without any reductions in the tariff; but after having made these reductions the remarkable thing is that the hon. member for Marquette decided to get out of the Government in any event. The hon. member, while he was a member of the Government of Canada for, I think, about a year and a half, occupied another position in this country. He was also President of .the Uniited Grain Growers, Limited. He was in the pay of the United Grain Growers, Limited of Canada, from whom he

was receiving a salary in excess of what he received as a member of the Government and a member of Parliament combined. The United Grain Growers, Limited, Mr. Speaker, has a system of recall embodied in their regulations; it is a part of their constitution. That is where the system of recall really originated in Canada. It is an American institution that has been brought over here, and it has been adopted in the regulations of the United Gram Growers, Limited. Let me point out this fact, Mr. Speaker, that we have the sworn evidence of the General Manager of the United Grain Growers, Limited that they endeavoured to put the recall into effect. Now, how did they put it into effect? How did_ they withdraw the president of 'heir company from the Government? I will tell you how they did it. I do not say that what I am about to state was the sole object of the hon. gentleman in deserting the Government. I say "deserting," because he as-su-edly did desert them before the task for vhich he was elected had been accomplished. There is no question about that. In September, 1918, the directors of the United Grain Growers, Limited passed a resolution or by-law whereby they increased the salary of the president, a member of the Government, from $10,000 to $15,000 a year, to go into effect when he withdrew from the Government. Apparently it was a very effective way of putting the Tecall into operation. Hon. gentlemen on cross benches opposite are subject to the recall, they may advocate a different kind, but this one evidently was quite effective in its operations, for it accomplished the Object at which it aimed, il want to make some further reference to Ithe hon. gentleman. The amalgamation of the Alberta Elevator Company and the Manitoba Grain Growers' Company into the United Grain Growers' Limited took place on the firjgt of September, 1917. The hon. gentleman, the president of this company, was sworn as a member of the Government on the 12th October, 1917. He resigned' 'from the Government on the 4th June, 1919. The hon. gentleman claims to have a particular interest in the farmers and that interest was shown on a number of occasions during the short time that he was Minister of Agriculture. A matter came up which was not of special interest to the grain growers of Western Canada as they were more interested in grain growing than anything else, tout which was of vital interest to the Dairymen of Eastern Canada as well as the West. An Order in Council was put through shortly after 
he became Minister of Agriculture permitting, strange to say, the great and wealthy corporations the packing houses on his license to gather up the dairy produce of the farmers of this country, mix it in their factories and sell it under another name. It lost its identity once it went into their factories and it came out as oleomargarine. I have referred to this matter in the past and I defy any one to say that I have ever objected to the importation or manufacture of oleomargarine. What I have objected to, what I do object to and I will continue to object to, is the great dairy industry being made a basis for the manufacture of this stuff and of secondary consideration to the big packing houses, and permitting them to gather up dairy produce and to treat it in such a way as to lose its identity the high standard which took so many years of industry to build up and to merge it with that of an inferior article. This was the first evidence that the hon. gentleman gave of his interest in agriculture.
But during all this time we had evidence that he was busy in another direction. In the province of Ontario the Provincial Government had been endeavouring to organize the farmers into clubs for co-operative purposes. There were also a few men who had been identified with farmers' movements in the years gone iby. We have had many farmers' organizations tin this country, political and ico-operative, that it is not easy to recall them all. We have had unrestricted reciprocity, commercial union, the patrons of industry and Dominion grange and others. A number of the old patrons of industry which was destroyed or absorbed by the Liberal Party in Ontario got together and endeavoured to prostitute or pervert the farmers' clubs. We have evidence published in a farming magazine that the hon. member for Marquette wa3 a frequent visitor at the offices of those who were furthering this movement in opposition to the farmers' co-operative clubs and the statement is also made that had it not been for the generous assistance in money and advice which this organization received from the grain growers of the West and the hon. member for Marquette they would not have .succeeded in their efforts. That has 'been published throughout the country by one of the original organizers of what is known as the United Farmers of Ontario. I often "wonder "whether this much lauded Grain Growers 'Limited had some ulterior object in view in endeavouring to destroy the co-operative spirit which was being created in Ontario.

It is absolutely impossible to divide the people of this country, to get people to organize Ithemselves along class lines politically in opposition to the interests of the /people of Canada generally. You may get a few designing ambitious individuals who regard their awn interests more that they do those of the class they claim to represent to take that stand, 'but I venture to state that inside of five years there will not be a vestige of that party left in this country. Why do I make such a statement as that? /Because I believe I know the farmers of [DOT]this country as well as does the hon. member for Marquette and I know that in so far as the province of Ontario is concerned the ease has been misrepresented Ito them.
That hon. gentleman in some of his addresses suggests to the farmers that they have not had a fair deal in the past, that they have not the representation in Parliament particularly in the House of Commons to which they are entitled. He even says that their representation is less than ten iper cent of the whole. The hon. gentleman is not always correct in the figures which he gives us. If you analyze the figures which the hon. gentleman put before the House a year ago when he endeavoured to justify his attitude, and if you inquire into many of the statements iwhich he has made in public you will find that you can discount them generally by aboult fifty per cent. I make the statement that the farmers have received generous treatment at the hands not only of this Government but of other governments in the redistribution of constituencies; representation has been in the farmers' favour. City constituencies have two and three times the population of rural on the whole.
What is going to be the upshot of this movement that is on foot led by the hon. member for Marquette? Do you suppose that the people of the towns and cities are going to sit ibaek and allow this condition to continue? The farmers of this country are organizing 'themselves into a political body and if that is the case and if they are going to separate themselves from other classes of the community there will only be one thing to do and we must have " representation according t-o population." This is the attitude that will be adopted. As far as the farmers of this country are concerned, they have had generous treatment at the hands of all governments with regard to parliamentary representation, I think that will be admitted by everybody. I know of counties which had three representatives in this House and 185
other constituencies which have only one representative although they have more votes than the county with three representatives. Is that fair if we are to have class representation because it happens to apply largely to rural districts? 1 represent a constituency myself where the vote is pretty evenly divided. There are a few more farmers than there are townspeople but I do not believe the people of my constituency have ever made any discrimination in that respect. I have received generous support from the people in the towns and I regret exceedingly that these hon. gentlemen opposite are not fair and do not give these people credit for having so acted in the past. If the farmers have not the representation in this House which they claim they are entitled to, they have nobody to blame but themselves. It is absolutely their own fault. They have often refused to vote for a candidate because he happened to be a farmer.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
An hon. gentleman says ''hear, hear." Yes, we will divide this country into classes in order to get the farmers to vote as a class but you ' are making the greatest mistake you ever made in your lives if you think the farmers are the narrow-minded, bigoted class you take them to be. The policy that you are advocating. class representation, may be adopted in some places but you will find that it will be spurned with indignation by the broadminded farmers of this country. It was during the most critical period in the history of this country-at a time when our eyes were fixed on the western battlefront, which was being day by day bent back, when every Canadian was almost afraid to road the morning papers for fear news of the line breaking-there were persons endeavouring to organize the farmers of Canada into a political organization, and some of them came trooping down to Ottawa asking that the farmers should be exempt from military service, and by their actions cast odium on the farmers of Ontario. But the people of that province were not responsible for what occurred at that time in connection with the question of military service. Hon. gentlemen opposite know full well that the executive which met in the city of Toronto, before coming down to Ottawa, were not honest with the people whom they claimed to represent. They claimed that they were coming down here ito endeavour to secure exemption from military service only in cases of extreme hardship, which would have been a very



(reasonable request and justifiable. Instead of that, however, they asked that total exemption should be granted to all farmers; and the man who is now sitting in this House as the representative for North Ontario, after having heard the Prime Minister state what the views of the Government were in regard to the matter, insisted upon coming before the Bar of the House of Commons in order to make a statement there. I will venture to state that under the circumstances no such proposition was ever dreamed of before. The men behind this request endeavoured to make it appear that a similar privilege had been granted to Mr. Gompers, the United States labour leader, and to Mr. Viviani, the exPrime Minister of France. But, Sir, on both those occasions the House had risen and was not actually in session when the distinguished men referred to addressed the members of Parliament. These are some of the things as to which the people of the province from which I come have been misled and misformed. These men went back .from the city of Ottawa and raised the cry, "Oh, we were turned out''; but the significant thing is that the Minister of Agriculture in the neighbouring province of Quebec wa6 one of the chief figures in that movement. In co-operation with some men who now have seats in this House the effort was made to make it appear that Ontario was responsible for the whole thing. Yes, there were a great many men from the western part of Ontario who were surprised when they got here at that time to find that there were so many delegates from other provinces.
Now, I must proceed to the consideration of other matters.

speechtext:
I am quite willing to be asked a question as to any matter arising out of my remarks.
I want briefly to refer to something that took place previous to the elections of 1917. There is in this country a publication known as the Canadian Annual Review, and I think every one will concede that it gives a very fair and impartial review of all matters of importance which transpire throughout Canada. This work, I believe, has now been conducted for about twenty years, and it certainly fills a want which was long felt before

that time. I want to quote from the Canadian Annual Review of 1917, page 594. Reference is there made to the attitude of the then leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) during the negotiations which led up to the formation of the Union Government, which he did not see fit to join, and in conclusion the following statement is made:
With it all the Liberal chieftain maintained his hopeful outlook, fought earnestly for his cherished convictions of a life-time, believed that he had a chance to win, and was convinced that if he did so the personal qualities and influence which had settled the Manitoba problem of 1896 could adjust those of 1917. If he did not win, his supporters, combined with the Liberals behind the Unionist Government, might be strong enough to revolutionize political conditions when the war rvas over.
Now, it may be possible that the right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier had some idea that that would happen. I think the events of the last few days would go to bear out the fact that he did show a good deal of foresight in that respect. We have found member after member-elected in support of Union Government-going over to the Opposition, and the excuse they make is that it is by reason of the tariff. Well, let me say, Mr. Speaker, that if any member of the House would be justified in breaking with the Government on the Tariff issue it would be those who are in favomr of the old protective policy-that policy which has been departed from by the Government in order to meet the demands or the requests of hon gentlemen on the cross benches. In order to carry on, and in order to insure that there should be harmony in this 'Country, the Government have 'conceded a good deal along this line. I am not saying that they have gone too far. I am not an extreme protectionist, I believe that a policy of moderate protection is necessary in this country; but I think the Government were entitled to some consideration from those hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred when in response to their wishes they conceded what they did in the matter of a reduction in the tariff. For example, two hon. gentlemen spoke in this House last week, and they took the ground that they were changing their political allegiance because of the fact that the tariff policy was now established and they could not see any hope for a reduction. Now the Government have made no such intimation either to the House or to the country. The Finance Minister has intimated-just as his predecessor intimated a year ago- that inquiries would be made into industrial

and other conditions after which the tariff would be readjusted to suit the conditions shown to exist. What more could be done than that? Of what use would it be to conduct an inquiry into Canadian conditions if you had settled upon your tariff policy before hand? The Government's tariff policy will depend upon the result of the inquiry which is to be made, and I aim strongly of the opinion that if it had not been for the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in the last Parliament, we would now have had a tariff commission that would have been able to place evidence before the Government, and this matter would have been dealt with ere this. However, that is the condition in which we find matters with respect to the tariff to-day. The tariff is the sole and absorbing topic of discussion by hon. gentlemen opposite. They are now endeavouring to justify the stand which they have taken. They are attempting to disorganize the Government of this country and make it impossible for the administration of public affairs to be carried on. The members of the so-called Agrarian party refer to the amendment of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) as a milk and water amendment, and they say that if he could have heard the Budget before he framed that amendment he never would have worded it in such a way. However, they were going to vote a want of confidence in the Government anyway, and so it did not matter much what the amendment contained. To those hon. gentlemen to whom I refer it does not matter what an amendment may contain so long as they can express a want of confidence in Sir Robert Borden and his Government. But that is not what the people are asking for; they are asking my hon. friends to be consistent. The hon. member for Marquette spoke for an hour and a half this afternoon, and the greater portion of his address was devoted to pointing out the ideal conditions hat exist in England, and then he suggested that agriculture should be looked after in this country. The hon. member has had the opportunity to acquire an intimate knowledge of Canadian agriculture, and if he takes the same interest in that industry which he claims he does he would have noticed that only within the last week efforts	were being made
in Great	Britain to	import into
that country breeding stock from Canada, but the British regulations will not permit it. It was admitted in the discussion which 185J
took place that the regulations with regard to cattle, which ostensibly were adopted in order to prevent foot and mouth disease reaching the cattle of Great Britain, were really uncalled for because there had never been a single case of the disease ini Canada; which went to show that the imposition of those regulations was mere camouflage, that in reality it was admitted a form of protection. But the farmers of Great Britain came to the conclusion that in special cases it would be advisable to permit the importation of cattle from Canada; they found from our dairy records that the butter fat production of some of our cows exceeded the best records of the cows of the Old Land by over 10,000 pounds per head.
Why don't they frankly admit that they have adopted protection so far as the farmers of Great Britain are concerned? The revenues collected there will indicate that in many inetances they have protection. Look at the	methods adopted to
check the importation of American automobiles: in order to enable the British automobile industry to get on its feet again the Government of Great Britain imposed what amounted to practically a prohibition on the importation of American automobiles. Those things have taken place in a country which for many years had a protective tariff, until Great. Britain obtained undisputed supremacy as a manufacturing country, and the peopte felt that they could remove the tariff and compete with the world. Their conditions were most favourable, for their manufacturing industries were well established and their commerce held undisputed sway on the high seas. But are conditions in Canada similar to those in Great Britain? When the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) says that we should have a fiscal policy identical with that which prevails in the Old Land, I would ask him if he would allow protection for some agricultural products, if necessary, such as has been adopted in Great Britain? I would point out, Sir, that people learn by experience, but the experience that costs something is the experience that is the most valuable to us.

Canada set about that development with a resolute spirit that commanded the admiration of the world. The duties on agricultural implements are held up as one of the oppressive handicaps that the agriculturist has to contend with. While the hon. member for Marquette was speaking I could not help thinking of some evidence given by the general manager of the United Grain Growers, Limited, a year ago to the effect that they had a great number of subsidiary companies. The hon. member for Marquette referred to one of those subsidiary companies this afternoon, which he stated on ,an investment of $100,000 had made profits in 1917 to the tune of $500,000. Surely a pretty good record. He endeavoured to remove the impression that that statement had made on the minds of a good many people by referring to the volume of business which the company transacted. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) also referred to that company in his speech the other night, and stated that the United Grain Growers, Limited, the parent company-he used the words " parent company " when referring to these profits of $500,000-had returned those profits into the pockets of the farmers. I want to take issue with the hon. member on that- point. The United Grain Growers, Limited, is an incorporated company on exactly the same footing as any other company, and it has not divided up its profits with the farmers. Nor is it doing so in connection with the profits of many of its subsidiary companies. The hon. member for Mackenzie piay know, because he is a director of the United Grain Growers, Limited, and he doubtless had good reason for qualifying his statement when he asserted that the parent ,company paid those profits back to the shareholders in dividends and cheaper machinery and so forth. As a matter of fact the shares of the United Grain Growers, Limited, were quoted at $25 a fMr. Sutherland.]
share, and I think the number any one shareholder can hold is limited to ten shares.

The tariff is the terrible bugbear of the farmers of the West we are told. Why did not the hon. member for Marquette and the hon. member for Mackenzie, the president and one of the prominent directors of the company, tell this House that the United Grain Growers, Limited, with their president a member of the Government, had purchased enormous quantities of American machinery a year ago and were holding them in bond expecting a reduction in the tariff at that time? Why was that statement not made to the House? A member of the Government president of the United Grain Growers. Limited, with inside 'information-his company profiting to that extent! I placed some questions on the Order Paper this (year with a view to ascertaining what amount of machinery had been so held by these people without result. But the evidence of the general manager of the United Grain Growers, Limited, shows that

the profits they made on the machinery which they imported into this country, I think it was in 1917, was 22.6 per cent. They do 'business with their customers on a spot cash basis. They have no agents. They have warehouses, and if a farmer wants a machine he can go there and get it, but he has to plank down the cash before he gets it,-and they simply charge him 22.6 per cent. He buys a binder for $250; the tariff at 124 per cent would be $31.25,-because a considerable reduction has been made in the tariff in order to meet the demands of such unreasonable gentlemen as the member for Marquette. I consider him unreasonable in that the pressure Which was brought to bear on 'the Government a year ago, when they conceded these things to him, should have (been sufficient to cause him to carry on and not try to disrupt and disorganize the Government at that time. Well, it is well known that binders and other like implements will with reasonable caTe, last fifteen years, so that the amount of duty when spread oveT the life of the binder is not very much,-$31.25 on a binder costing $250. But the hon. member for Marquette did not point out that the United Grain Growers, Limited, want $52.87 profit on that binder from the farmer who is he claims benefited by the profits made by this company. Where do .all these surplus profits go? And there are other subsidiary 'Companies as well. I am afraid that I shall not be able to get through before six o'clock, but I want to assure you that other matters in connection with the administration of the Department of Agriculture while the president of the United Grain Growers, Limited, was in the pay of that company and a member of the Government will require some investigation before this Parliament prorogues- an investigation to which the people of Canada are entitled.
